# Neurodegeneration and Mendelian disease

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/07-neuro-mendelian.yml` and not yet reviewed by a second
reader.
:::

This is where isoform biology has gone furthest into the clinic.
Splicing-directed drugs hold approval in two diseases, a cryptic exon has
become a pathology-specific marker, and a splice-modulating oligonucleotide has
been designed for a single patient. It is also where the field disagrees most
sharply about how large the underlying phenomenon is.

## The brain splices more than other tissues {#sec-brain-splicing}

Of the human tissues compared on genomically aligned EST evidence, brain
carried the highest fraction of alternatively spliced genes. More than 40 per
cent of its genes showed at least one alternative splicing event, ahead of
liver and testis [@yeo2004tissuesplicing].

The synaptic adhesion molecules are the extreme case. Neurexin mRNAs are
alternatively spliced at six canonical positions, SS1 through SS6, whose use is
tightly regulated in space and time [@trotter2023neurexin3].

Long reads have raised the scale again. Sequencing of mid-gestation human
neocortex reported 214,516 distinct isoforms, 72.6 per cent of them unannotated
in GENCODE, plus more than 7,000 novel exons. That expanded the inferred
proteome by 92,422 putative proteoforms from one developing tissue
[@patowary2024neocortexisoforms].

## Tau and a ratio the cell has to hold {#sec-mapt}

Adult human brain holds 3R-tau and 4R-tau at roughly a one-to-one ratio.
Whether MAPT exon 10 is included or skipped is what sets that balance, because
that exon encodes the second microtubule-binding repeat
[@liu2008tauexon10].

Eleven FTDP-17 mutations fall inside a single self-complementary stem loop
spanning the exon 10 and intron 10 boundary. Each disrupts the complementarity
and destabilises the structure. The same position is already destabilised in
rodents, which is offered as the reason adult mice and rats are predominantly
4R [@liu2008tauexon10].

Two neighbouring mutations push in opposite directions. N279K and delta-280K
sit in the same polypurine enhancer of exon 10, adding or deleting an AAG copy
respectively, which raises or lowers SF2/ASF binding [@liu2008tauexon10].

The decisive observation is that some of these mutations are silent or
intronic. They disrupt exon 10 splicing without altering tau's primary
sequence, which makes an altered 3R:4R ratio sufficient on its own to cause
neurodegeneration and dementia. Most such mutations push toward 4R, a minority
toward 3R [@liu2008tauexon10]. Both directions are pathogenic, so the
phenotype is the ratio rather than either isoform.

## TDP-43 and exons that should not exist {#sec-tdp43}

TDP-43's role in splicing is negative, in that it suppresses the splicing of
non-conserved cryptic exons and so preserves intron integrity. When it is
depleted, those exons enter mRNAs, frequently disrupting translation and
triggering nonsense-mediated decay, and that repression is already impaired in
ALS-FTD cases [@ling2015crypticexons].

### STMN2

In STMN2 the pathogenic event is a change in RNA processing rather than a
mutation. When TDP-43 levels fall, its binding to the first intron is lost, a
cryptic polyadenylation site there is used, and the gene produces a truncated
transcript that is not functional [@melamed2019stathmin2].

The association with disease is close to absolute. Exon 2a was present in
laser-captured lumbar motor neurons from every one of thirteen sporadic ALS
patients examined. It was absent from all seven non-ALS individuals tested
[@melamed2019stathmin2].

The lesion carries the phenotype rather than accompanying it. Re-expressing
stathmin-2 from a construct lacking the cryptic polyadenylation site restored
axonal regeneration after axotomy in TDP-43-depleted human iPSC motor neurons,
even though TDP-43 affects the levels or splicing of many RNAs
[@melamed2019stathmin2].

There is a reason this took so long to find. Neither the cryptic polyadenylation
signal nor the three GU-rich TDP-43 binding sites of human STMN2 intron 1 exist
in the corresponding mouse intron. The abnormal processing is correspondingly
not reproduced in TDP-43 transgenic or TDP-43-deficient mice
[@melamed2019stathmin2], so the mechanism is absent from the standard model
organism.

### UNC13A

Cryptic exon de-repression on TDP-43 loss is broad and lands on a known risk
gene only rarely. Of 179 cryptic exons detected in TDP-43-depleted
iPSC-derived cortical-like neurons, the synaptic gene UNC13A was the only host
gene that was also an established ALS-FTD risk gene [@brown2022unc13a].

![The same cryptic exon across diagnostic groups. Groups with no detections are
shown as labelled zeroes rather than omitted, because the absences are what
make this a marker of TDP-43 pathology rather than of
neurodegeneration.](../figures/unc13a-specificity.svg){#fig-unc13a width=100%}

In 1,349 post-mortem brain and spinal cord tissues from 377 individuals, the
UNC13A cryptic exon was found only in TDP-43 proteinopathy. It appeared in 89
per cent of FTLD-TDP and 38 per cent of ALS-TDP individuals, and in no SOD1 or
FUS ALS case, no FTLD-TAU or FTLD-FUS case, and no control
[@brown2022unc13a].

That same exon resolves a long-unexplained GWAS association. The top ALS- and
FTD-associated variants at UNC13A lie inside the intron that harbours the
cryptic exon rather than in coding sequence, and they increase cryptic exon
splicing when TDP-43 is dysfunctional [@ma2022unc13a]. Patient tissues
homozygous for the risk alleles showed significantly more cryptic exon
inclusion even after normalising to STMN2 cryptic splicing, which controls for
how much TDP-43 function each sample had already lost [@brown2022unc13a].

A GWAS hit, a mechanism and a pathology-specific marker turn out to be the same
intron.

## Spinal muscular atrophy: two drugs on one exon {#sec-sma}

SMN2 is a nearly identical copy of SMN1 that fails to compensate for its loss,
because it predominantly skips exon 7. The change held responsible is a single
C-to-T substitution at the sixth nucleotide of that exon, proposed to weaken
its 3' splice site [@singh2020risdiplam].

Both approved splicing-directed drugs act on that one exon. Nusinersen is an
antisense oligonucleotide targeting the intronic splicing silencer ISS-N1 in
SMN2, and is described as the first FDA-approved drug for SMA. Risdiplam, an
orally deliverable small molecule, became the third approved SMA therapy
[@singh2020risdiplam].

The trial results are worth stating with their denominators. In the phase 3
sham-controlled trial of nusinersen in infants, the final analysis recorded a
motor-milestone response in 37 of 73 treated infants, which is 51 per cent, and
in none of the 37 controls [@finkel2017endear]. In FIREFISH Part 1, 41 per cent
of infants with type 1 SMA given the therapeutic dose of risdiplam, 7 of 17,
could sit independently for at least five seconds at twelve months
[@belancic2025smatrials].

Risdiplam raises full-length SMN protein by promoting exon 7 inclusion, is
taken once daily by mouth, and received EMA approval in March 2021 on the basis
of the FIREFISH and SUNFISH trials [@belancic2025smatrials].

## Duchenne: skipping an exon on purpose {#sec-dmd}

The therapeutic logic came from reading a natural experiment. DMD deletions that
leave the reading frame intact generate variants able to produce a functional if
truncated dystrophin, and the milder Becker phenotype. That is read as showing
that the nature of the deletion determines severity [@lim2017eteplirsen].
Removing more sequence can therefore help, if what is removed restores the
frame.

Four exon-skipping antisense drugs hold FDA approval on that basis. These were
accelerated approvals resting mainly on a biomarker, modest increases in
dystrophin, and that basis is described as having sparked significant debate
[@moriyama2026dmdaso].

## How much of inherited disease runs through splicing {#sec-mendelian-fraction}

The published estimates do not converge, and the reason is that they are
answers to different questions.

A machine-learning estimate over exonic variants put the splice-disrupting
fraction at approximately 16 per cent of inherited disease exonic mutations,
and approximately 10 to 14 per cent of cancer exonic mutations. That share is
predicted rather than assayed, and covers exonic variants only
[@mort2014mutpredsplice].

A massively parallel splicing assay measured it directly. Of 4,964 exonic
disease alleles drawn from HGMD, about 10 per cent, 513 of them, disrupted
splicing both in cells and in vitro, against 3 per cent of the common SNPs
tested the same way [@soemedi2017mapsy].

The SpliceAI authors put cryptic splicing behind 9 to 11 per cent of
pathogenic mutations in rare disease patients. They describe that as a class of
disease variation the field had underappreciated [@jaganathan2019spliceai].

The familiar one-third figure does not belong in this list. It enters the
literature as one group's summary of previous studies rather than as a
measurement they report, so it should not be counted as an independent estimate
[@soemedi2017mapsy].

Splice-region variants have been apportioned between positions directly. A de
novo mutation burden analysis across 7,833 developmental disorder
probands and their parents gave 73 per cent of the pathogenic contribution to
the canonical dinucleotides, and 27 per cent to flanking non-canonical positions
[@lord2019splicesites].

That non-canonical share is itself contested by more than twofold. The same
paper's discussion sets its trio-based 27 per cent against three others: roughly
30 per cent from HGMD, roughly 43 per cent from another curation, and roughly 17
per cent in ClinVar. It attributes the spread to how each set's variants were
ascertained [@lord2019splicesites], which means ascertainment orders those four
numbers.

## RNA sequencing as a diagnostic {#sec-rnaseq-diagnosis}

The incremental yield over exome sequencing has been measured several times,
and the tissue explains much of the spread.

Muscle RNA sequencing of 50 genetically undiagnosed rare muscle disease
patients reached an overall diagnosis rate of 35 per cent. It got there by
validating candidate splice-disrupting variants, and by finding variants that
altered splicing from exonic positions and from deep inside introns
[@cummings2016musclernaseq].

Fibroblasts give a lower number for mitochondrial disease. Transcriptome
sequencing of 48 exome-undiagnosed mitochondriopathy patients produced a
molecular diagnosis in 10 per cent, 5 of 48, and candidate genes for the
remainder. Per-sample medians were one aberrantly expressed gene and five
aberrant splicing events [@kremer2017rnaseqdiagnosis]. The same approach was
then scaled into a clinical workflow. Skin fibroblasts from 303 individuals with
suspected mitochondrial disease who had already had exome sequencing gave a
genetic diagnosis in 16 per cent of the 205 exome-inconclusive cases
[@yepez2022rnaseqclinical].

Targeted long reads reach cases with no candidate gene at all. A disease-panel
assay produced molecular diagnoses in two such patients, including a Leigh
syndrome case resolved by two unproductive MTFMT splicing events, partial exon
4 skipping and a 53-bp pseudoexon in intron 6 [@wang2026stripe].

Long reads are not uniformly better than short ones. Across 27 distinct splicing
outcomes
collated from short- and long-read data in a rare disorder cohort, PacBio
long-read RNA-seq recovered 18 variant-linked aberrant splicing events and
three normal outcomes, and failed to capture four. Three of the four are
attributed to low or absent coverage of the gene [@oquendo2026hifirnaseq].
Coverage of the specific disease gene mattered more than read length in
those four cases.

## Prediction tools rank better than they quantify {#sec-splice-prediction}

Interpretation now leans on tools whose accuracy has been measured against
experimentally characterised variants. On NF1 spliceogenic variants, SpliceAI
reached an ROC area under the curve of 0.972 for de novo or cryptic splice site
prediction. That was ahead of every other tool tested except SpliceRover at
0.924. The difference from SpliceRover was not statistically significant
[@jang2022splicetools].

Agreement with measured effects is lower than those curves suggest. On the
OpenSplice massively parallel reporter benchmark, SpliceAI2 agreed with
experimentally measured variant effects at Spearman 0.59, against 0.55 for
SpliceAI [@jaganathan2026spliceai2]. Ranking variants and predicting their
quantitative effect are different tasks, and the tools are much better at the
first.

## One patient, one drug {#sec-nof1}

The endpoint of isoform-level diagnosis is a drug designed for one genome.
Proof-of-concept experiments in cell lines from a single patient were the basis
for launching an n-of-1 study of the splice-modulating oligonucleotide milasen,
within one year of first contact with that patient [@kim2019milasen].

The clinical result was partial, with seizure frequency and duration falling to
half their pre-treatment values. The drug did not impede progressive brain
volume loss, and the patient died three years after treatment began
[@wiltonclark2024nof1aso].

The route from a splicing lesion to a molecule that corrects it is now short
enough to run inside a year. Whether correcting the lesion reverses the disease
is a separate question, and this case answered it partly.
